title: Indian Banks Collected Over Rs 7,000 Crore From Account Holders for Low Balance Penalties in FY26
excerpt: The practice continues to burden small depositors despite several public sector banks waiving minimum balance charges in the past year.
body:
• Indian banks collected over Rs 7,000 crore from savings account holders in FY26 as penalties for not maintaining the required minimum balance.
  • Public sector banks alone collected nearly Rs 9,000 crore in such charges over the five years from FY21 to FY25, according to Finance Ministry data presented in Parliament.
  • Several banks — including SBI, PNB, Canara Bank and Indian Bank — have recently waived minimum balance requirements, but private banks continue to levy significant charges.
  • Approximately 72 crore basic savings accounts, including Jan Dhan accounts, are exempt from these penalties.

The Scale of the Problem

Indian banks collected over Rs 7,000 crore from account holders in the financial year ending March 2026 for failing to maintain minimum monthly average balances in their savings accounts, continuing a practice that has drawn criticism from consumer advocates and parliamentarians.

The figure adds to a troubling pattern. Finance Ministry data presented in the Rajya Sabha showed that 11 public sector banks alone collected nearly Rs 9,000 crore in such penalties over the five-year period from FY21 to FY25. Private sector banks collected an additional Rs 11,000 crore over just three years, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

""This move is aimed at fostering financial inclusion and making banking more accessible and affordable for all sections of society," the bank said in July 2025."

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman told Parliament that the charges constituted approximately 0.23 percent of public sector banks' total income during the period, describing them as "primarily aligned with the cost of providing banking services rather than revenue generation through penalties."

Who Bears the Burden

The penalties disproportionately affect small depositors — students, daily wage earners, senior citizens and rural account holders who may not track their balances closely. Minimum balance requirements vary by bank and branch location, ranging from Rs 2,500 in rural areas to Rs 10,000 in metropolitan branches. Penalties for falling below the threshold can range from Rs 100 to Rs 500 per month.

The Reserve Bank of India does not set a uniform minimum balance. Individual banks determine their own requirements and penalty structures. However, the RBI mandates that banks notify customers through SMS, email or letter before applying charges and give them time to restore the balance.

Wave of Waivers

Several major public sector banks moved to eliminate minimum balance charges over the past year. SBI discontinued monthly minimum balance penalties in March 2020. Punjab National Bank, Canara Bank and Indian Bank followed in mid-2025, waiving charges across all savings accounts.

Indian Bank's announcement was typical of the shift. "This move is aimed at fostering financial inclusion and making banking more accessible and affordable for all sections of society," the bank said in July 2025.

The RBI's Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account (BSBDA) scheme, which eliminates minimum balance requirements entirely, now covers approximately 72 crore accounts, including those opened under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana.

What NRIs Should Know

For Non-Resident Indians maintaining savings or NRO accounts in India, minimum balance penalties can quietly erode dormant accounts. Many NRIs discovered unexpected deductions when reviewing accounts during visits home. The waiver trend among public sector banks is encouraging, but private banks — where many NRIs hold accounts — continue to levy charges. Account holders should check their bank's current policy and consider converting to a BSBDA if eligible.
nri_angle: NRIs maintaining Indian bank accounts face minimum balance penalties that can quietly drain dormant accounts, making the policy personally relevant to the diaspora.
author: Diaspora Desk
